title: INSERT Statement & RETURNING Clause
description: Insert single and multiple rows, insert from queries, and retrieve generated keys using PostgreSQL's powerful RETURNING clause.

data.text: The **`INSERT`** statement adds new rows to a table. While standard SQL requires issuing a secondary query to fetch auto-generated IDs, PostgreSQL pioneered the **`RETURNING`** clause, allowing you to return inserted column values, computed defaults, or full row tuples in a single atomic roundtrip.

data.title: Multi-Row Insert Returning Generated UUIDs
data.content: Inserts multiple rows and immediately returns the generated primary keys and timestamps.
data.code:
INSERT INTO users (email, name, role)
VALUES 
    ('alice@company.com', 'Alice Smith', 'ADMIN'),
    ('bob@company.com', 'Bob Jones', 'STAFF'),
    ('carol@company.com', 'Carol White', 'CUSTOMER')
RETURNING id, email, created_at;

data.text: You can populate a table directly from the result of a `SELECT` query, which executes entirely within the database engine without sending data across the network.

data.title: Archiving Stale Inactive Users
data.content: Copying data from an active table to an archive table.
data.code:
INSERT INTO archived_users (user_id, email, archived_at)
SELECT id, email, NOW()
FROM users
WHERE last_login_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '365 days'
RETURNING user_id;

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...), (...)` for efficient batch insertion.
Use `RETURNING *` or `RETURNING id` to eliminate secondary `SELECT` lookups.
`INSERT INTO ... SELECT` allows high-speed server-side data transformation.
